189.s: Handy called him a rock and roll player; he says it was bebop versus Dixieland.
189.q: No, see when I started playing, see all those guys had a certain style they played, and I played different styles. And they didn't like me because when I called all of them up to a Muhammad, I didn't want to play with them anymore because they're not playing bebop.

189.t: Bebop's lack of public audience and Louis Jordan
189.s: No clubs for bebop, people could not dance to it; Louis Jordan's small band broke up big bands.
189.q: It wasn't. Just among musicians, all the musicians. Like if you didn't play bebop, you were in the square. The guys your age wouldn't be bothered with you. So it was just sort of in the musicians themselves,

107.t: Bebop attitude and the public's rejection of it
107.s: Bebop made him more analytical, but friends, his father, girls and club owners disliked it and wanted dance music like The Hucklebuck.
107.q: I had a new attitude about being a musician. I had the conception that this music was taking me forward. It absorbed me so much that I became a lot more passionate about the music, a lot more concerned about knowing what the inner workings of this music was. Before I just performed. I enjoyed, and…

107.t: Bebop as culture and catalyst at a vulnerable age
107.s: Brower frames bebop as attitude, dress and black cultural expression, and Foster explains why he was open to it and followed Parker, Gillespie, Monk and Roach.
107.q: It caught me at a time when I was able to adjust from whatever I was doing totally to that movement, bebop, and get into it fully. I was at the age when I was most --

64.t: Roots, anointed leaders, Cecil Taylor and owning the music
64.s: He says Parker and Gillespie stayed rooted in tradition, critics wrongly anoint leaders, and bebop reclaimed Black-created music from white bands.
64.ch: Harlem ideas and bebop as revolution
64.q: Duke Ellington and others. What they did was to take… Duke Ellington was a revolutionary. I mean when he started talking about black beauty back in ‘29, when he was talking about in the ‘40s, the kind of parallel to the history of his entire race, he was doing the kind of thing that was giving the…

64.t: Was modern jazz a revolution or an evolution?
64.s: Taylor argues bebop was evolution built on elders like Lester Young and Hawkins, though revolutionary in how it changed the rhythm section.
64.ch: Harlem ideas and bebop as revolution
64.q: Not in that sense. It was evolution and it was firmly… it was a revolution in the sense that what was necessary was to discard certain things out of the past in order to make the present work on the highest level. So that meant you had to change what the drummer did, that meant you had to change…

9.t: How bop changed the music, and why he did not like it
9.s: He first heard bop in the early Forties at Minton's, found it 'for the birds', and preferred gutbucket jazz you can tap your foot to.
9.ch: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
9.q: : What do you mean? Oh yes, the music had changed. It started changing when I... The music started changing before I even got with Cootie's band, and that was in the early Forties. It started changing then. They were doing some Bop then, back in them days, with ...(?)... thing, and in Minton's Bar.…

9.t: Charlie Ventura's bop band replaced by Kirby in Milwaukee
9.s: The Milwaukee club hated Ventura's bebop, which Holmes admired, and hired Kirby's popular-song band to finish the engagement.
9.ch: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
9.q: : In the meantime, Charlie Ventura's band opened in... I will call this club the Cosmopolitan Club in Milwaukee. That's not the name of it, but that's what I'll call it -- because I don't remember the name of it! Anyway, Charlie Ventura's band followed Kirby's band in there. Well, Kirby had a band…

146.t: Smith's reaction to Bebop and young players
146.s: Smith thought Bebop was technical and would ruin young players who could not play it; his band's soloists took advantage.
146.ch: Looking back and the New York years
146.q: I said, 'Well, that's all right. It's very technical. Ain't nobody gonna be able to play it but a real artist.' And I said, 'That's going to ruin a whole lot of these young musicians around here' -- which it did. I knew that was going to happen.

146.t: Bebop-minded players in his Dallas band
146.s: Smith says young players in his band thought themselves bebop but lacked substance, though a few such as Curtis White were good.
146.ch: Dallas bands, Ray Charles and family
146.q: Yeah. We had two or three of them in there. We had a trumpet player I was telling you about a while ago in that band, and a tenor player. Yeah, they was goin' wild!

147.t: What bothered him about bebop drummers
147.s: Crawford says bebop drummers got out of hand and called it noise, naming Clarke and Roach as all-around drummers and Roy Haynes a combo drummer.
147.ch: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
147.q: The drummers and the players. I didn't like it at first, and happened to be -- I happened to listen a little bit more, don't like it right now. I'm as I forestated a swinger, (inaudible).

147.t: Disliking bebop; Art Blakey, Max Roach and Kenny Clarke
147.s: Crawford says he preferred swinging and did not care for bebop but admired Blakey, Roach and his friend Kenny Clarke.
147.ch: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
147.q: if I had the execution that Art Blakey's got, I don't know where he came from. He just came up, and he can play. Beautiful drummer, accents and whatnot. I don't know where he came from, but that rascal sure can play. Max Roach and all that batch, Max [got something from them too]. (Inaudible) Oh,…

385.t: How bebop developed and came to be accepted
385.s: He argues Parker and Dizzy were born to it and joined by fate, that the younger musicians put it across, and discusses peers' envy.
385.q: ... determination ... ... I couldn't go to school because... they don't teach 4 string... then I would have to try to switch to 6 string, and by the time I get anywhere, I'd be so far behind that... peers... they ready to step on my nose right now if they can. They always are. You do anything…

385.t: How musicians reacted to Bird; who named bebop
385.s: Most players said bebop was Chinese music because they could not play it; Grimes says he helped introduce Dizzy at the Apollo.
385.q: Oh yeah, it was knocke'd, it was nearly a strike. I mean, the guys, they couldn't play it see, cause they were still into Dixieland really, just out of Dixieland was Basie and Ellington, the way we played, and Eddie they went with Ben Webster. A few other groups even Stuff Smith & Eddie -- South.…

78.s: Horace admired Parker and Dizzy (whom he heard at Minton's) but could not play bebop and, on Fletcher's advice, stuck to swing and standards.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: Tom, I hate to say this, but bebop never moved me. Number one is I couldn't play it, and I used to fool around and try to play some things. I learned in later years to play it a little, but I was told to stick more or less to the swing, you know? And while I admired Charlie Parker. I had nothing…

78.t: Trying bebop on audiences; analyzing 'Night in Tunisia'; Hawkins plays bop
78.s: Dancers walked off when he played bop; he learned the notes by testing chords against 'A Night in Tunisia'. Hawkins eventually played it well, but Horace insists you must know your instrument.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: And if I -- I had a few bebop numbers in my group, but I tested this out, and I played places. We played bebop, and some of the people looked at us like we were crazy. They'd walk off the floor. After, I previously played just a little old, hard kind of standard tune, and they liked it. Soon as I…

590.t: How Armstrong's music changed with big bands; his view of bop
590.s: Louis played pop tunes and had to change when playing with big bands; he did not play bop, but bop players studied him.
590.q: Well, Louis did. Louis used to like to play pop latoons as well as, yeah. Many people wanted Louis to go back and play things that he played 50 years.

49.t: Three changes in jazz and first hearing Dizzy Gillespie in Chicago
49.s: Hazel sees ragtime, pure jazz and bop as successive changes, and recounts hearing Gillespie's group in Chicago.
49.q: It reminds me of the way I look at this progressive music all the way. This is the third change that I've seen. The first was, some people like to call it ragtime, and then came what they used to laughingly call the pure jazz.

591.t: Disagreement with Delaunay over modern jazz
591.s: He recounts Delaunay playing Gillespie and Parker and objects to dissonance without resolution, citing his teacher.
591.q: Well, my opinion... I told Dolaunay in Paris, when he brought in those records from Gillespie over, he called me up and told me to come up and listen to him. Yeah. And I spent about two hours at the hot club of Paris, which he called himself the President of... Yeah. And I listened to it. I didn't…

572.s: He says bebop plays many notes without melody and prefers to make people happy.
572.ch: Wider talk: bands, places and players
572.q: But, uh, since then, uh, music has changed so much now, and, and now, now they, they got this, uh, the, uh, what the, what the hell they call them, uh, Park, or what the hell they call them, uh.

23.t: Bop and Leonard Feather; musicians don't theorize
23.s: Rose says bop has no jazz derivation and attacks Leonard Feather's integrity. He says musicians want jobs, not theory, and one pianist told him jazz is whatever a jazz musician plays.
23.q: Of course. Keep in mind that we're not talking about an area in which I am an expert. We're only talking about my tastes and speculation.

58.s: Miller plays a bop number and they discuss it.
58.ch: Making up numbers, bop and technique
58.q: Well I mean them places, they're the drawing of people in. Yeah. They don't want that in there that's causing me. But I'm talking about just a complete dance hall. Mm-hmm. While you're playing a dance and trying to get some, you know, nice music out of it. He used to do it. Dick, I'm gonna put…

434.t: Bebop, teenagers and the decline of jazz's popularity
434.s: Allen says bop lost the teenage dance audience, exempts Charlie Parker and Supersax, and lists other reasons jazz lost popularity.
434.ch: The Golden Age and what followed
434.q: All of the above. A very good question. I love all kinds of jazz. I love some kinds a little more than the other, but I’ve never heard jazz where I would say that is rotten, get rid of it. I just love jazz. Boom. But one form that I enjoy, which is bop or progressive or bebop, is clearly, I don’t…

132.t: Bebop in the press in the late 1940s
132.s: Press then was about the big bands' decline; Dizzy and Parker appear only in the 1950s.
132.ch: Opinions on jazz and big bands
132.q: I think in the ‘50s yeah, but in the late ‘40’s no. The press had to do mostly with the downfall of the big bands. And I guess Dizzy got some press. But if you look at the Down Beat and Metronome contest for the musician of the year you won’t find Dizzy in those years. You will in the 50s, you’ll…

329.s: Hanna calls most bop players corny, excepting Charlie Parker, Conte Candoli, Sonny Berman and Red Rodney.
329.q: I mean that’s phenomenal. But most of those bop guys were corny, man, they didn’t swing or anything. It just sounded like they didn’t know what they were doing. And I don’t think they did. No these guys were superb, you know, superb. But these guys played what they called bop I guess, Sonny Berman…

332.t: Why bebop had a smaller popular audience
332.s: Ingham thinks bebop was urban small-group music with no whistleable tunes, contrasted with songs like 'Blues in the Night'.
332.ch: Learning and views on jazz history
332.q: I think it had a small audience — well I say small — I mean it certainly took off in a way I think, when you look back on it, but it was the urban areas. I mean first of all there were some big bands of course, like Billy Eckstine’s band and Dizzy Gillespie took a big band out. But they were…

356.s: Bop was confusing at first but hip; Roy Eldridge's Rocking Chair.
356.q: Oh boy I’d love to get a copy of that. That’s one of the great records of all time.

362.t: Fusion generation, boring bebop records and hearing Barry Harris live
362.s: Raised on fusion, he found short bebop records dull until hearing Barry Harris live in 1982; recording limits shaped Japanese bebop.
362.q: No. When I came in the eighties he was still around. But in the eighties I was kind of more like a new kind of jazz. I started appreciating this kind of style more after I was over 40. So now I am 55, and like 15 years ago I started listening to really old style of jazz. Because my generation was…

365.t: State of jazz, early bop, Monroe's Uptown House and Benny Carter
365.s: He compares today's youngsters to the bop generation, recalls Dizzy's early bop around Monroe's versus Minton's, and joining Benny Carter.
365.q: It’s the same as it’s always been with youngsters coming up with new ideas. I know when — I’m from more or less the bop era, and the older guys didn’t understand what we were doing and we didn’t know what we were doing either, but we were doing something you know? It evolved into bop. Well the kids…

101.t: Leaving the Navy and keeping to his own style amid bebop
101.s: Out of the Navy in 1945, back to Hudson; Terry did not copy bebop but admired it.
101.q: I suppose when I first started listening to it, when it first became on the scene. I never was one to really jump up and copy things, but I would love the way it sounded. I was always browbeaten by some of the people who would talk to me. They said,

16.s: He recalls hearing Dizzy, Klook and Parker at the Famous Door on furlough, being stunned, and sees bebop as a kind of black backlash.
16.q: If I'm understanding you correctly, I'm not exactly sure that's the issue. I think that yes, I don’t know that they were building like our parents, but I think that what they were doing was

225.s: Johnson explains why bringing winners together never produced memorable music.
225.q: I remember more of how I felt about the outcome of those gatherings than anything else. The results were not always what I would have imagined would happen.

104.t: Jimmy's view of bebop and her own bebop arrangements for his band
104.s: Jimmy felt committed to his style and thought bebop was too many notes; in the late 1940s she wrote bebop arrangements for his band, and he struggled to play 'Manteca' for an act.
104.q: Yeah, but he was . . . he admitted that he was . . . he felt that he was committed to the style that he played. I think a lot of the . . . even sometimes with Dizzy, he would say, “It seems that all they do is play a lot of notes.” And yet when anybody would play a beautiful ballad or something, he…

123.t: What the Bird celebration plays and what bebop is
123.s: He says the month features Bird and bebop tunes, and insists bebop is more than fast notes.
123.q: Just coming in and playing the tunes Bird was associated with. Or the bebop stuff like Monk, Bud Powell, Tadd Dameron, you know. Fats Navarro, that kind of stuff. Like I always say, like Dexter used to say, “bebop is the future.” And I always add, “as soon as they learn how to play it.” I said,…

1.t: The pianist turns bopper and the boppers' new Muslim names
1.s: The pianist, hanging out with Louis Metcalf, joined the bop musicians who took new names and a Muslim society.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: Yeah, from Detroit. He was out at this... Well, he was with me. He said, 'Man, what are you talkin' about? You gotta play this music.' He said, 'I ain't playin' no more Blues.' He said, 'Well, lay out.' So he sat there. And he started hanging out. He'd met some musicians from New York that was…

67.t: Reaction to bebop and Parker and Dizzy
67.s: Players feared they were finished, many trumpeters lost their minds, and Cheatham could not understand it then but now likes it.
67.ch: Teddy Wilson, Cafe Society and bebop
67.q: Well, after -- as soon as Charlie Parker and Dizzy got together. Then they started to -- recording that they made together. That's when I first realized that things were changing.

68.t: Why many older musicians put bebop down
68.s: Tate liked the bebop players, but did not try to play that way, and cannot see why others put it down.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: Then, of course, he continued to play. I mean, we'd jam down there at night and he was playing -- by then, he was playing what he wanted -- his style then, you know, but it hadn't really caught on with the people.

166.t: His view that bop was made to exclude jam-session players
166.s: He argues that bop's changed harmonies were meant to stop outsiders from stealing Black music.
166.ch: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
166.q: -- was writing for Benny Goodman, making him a swing band, you know, like Edgar Sampson and Jimmy Mundy, they were writing all these swing arrangements for Benny Goodman. And down on 52nd Street they was letting the Caucasians come and sit in, you know, trying to steal our music. And a lot of them…

379.t: Why he did not like Gillespie's big band
379.s: He says the music was too advanced for the available musicians.
379.ch: Dizzy, Chano Pozo and Afro-Cuban jazz
379.q: There was -- I tell you why I didn't like the band. Maybe I didn't hear enough of the band. I just had the band. But even when Chano was there, to me this was not jazz, and the music was (inaudible) for the band. The music was too advanced (inaudible) for the material he have to work with.

167.t: Bebop as changes without melody; Dizzy Gillespie
167.s: Bunn calls bop musicians' music with weird notes and no melody, started by Dizzy Gillespie and copied by everyone.
167.q: Just like different songs that's come out before that bop did come out. Understand? The songs was gone, but yet still he come out and that changed the trend of all things.

28.t: Dizzy as pathfinder; melody, pit jobs and Black players
28.s: Dizzy changed the instrument like Hawkins, but followers cannot play melody, and Black musicians are excluded from pit bands and hotel jobs; Butler complains of Fiedler and Lawrence Welk.
28.q: No. Dizzy -- Dizzy man, everybody knows that. He changed the instrument. He changed -- he changed that instrument. He was the first one. He changed it. See? He changed the whole panorama -- he changed it. See, he was a pathfinder.

382.s: In the mid-1950s she listened to Dizzy at the Royal Roost and wasn't impressed at first, but accepts it created a new sound.
382.q: Well, way back, I would say around 1956, before I eventually retired, I was appearing at the Village Vanguard down in the Village; and a friend of mine came and said, 'I want to take you uptown to hear the new music.'

71.s: They agree that turning one's back and not announcing numbers was rude behavior after bop.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: Oh very rude, yes. In other words, you are lucky to be there. You are lucky to listen to me play. No matter if I turn my back on you, that's the attitude they used to have.

18.t: Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and bebop
18.s: He never met Parker, was buddies with Dizzy, whom he told was spoiling musicians.
18.q: : In the beginning I didn't like Dizzy's playing because he spoiled a whole lot of musicians. That's when this Juilliard thing started, you know, he'd put on his beret and go around with his horn and everyone wanted to do a Dizzy... I told him, "You're spoiling the other musicians. You're too great…

92.t: How music changed with bebop; meeting Sarah Vaughan
92.s: Postwar music had fast, changing tempos and was for listening, not dancing; Collins felt at home, and Dameron introduced him to Sarah Vaughan.
92.ch: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
92.q: Oh, everything that had happened. It was no -- I mean, it was all bebop. Now, the whole structure of music had changed, and here's Dizzy again. Dizzy and Bird, the tempos were super-fast, like before when I went into the army people would dance. Nobody danced any more now, they -- everything was a…

72.s: He found Parker, Gillespie and Monk's music different but still real music.
72.ch: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
72.q: Well, to me, I didn't... I couldn't get it under my finger just what it was. But it was music, but it was a different style. I always recognized a tune, you might play a little melody once in a while. But if you didn't know what number that was playing, you wouldn't... You know. All of it sounded…

384.t: His opinion of bebop and love of Dixieland
384.s: In the 1950 article he dismisses bebop as discord and praises the Dixie two-beat as being part of a happy throbbing machine.
384.ch: N'goma drums and the scrapbook clippings
384.q: As for the newest fad in popular music, bebop, Morehouse hasn't a great deal of love for it. "There are always fads in the arts," he said, "and in our music bop is the latest.

412.t: The split between bebop and traditional players
412.s: DeMichael asks about Charlie Parker and Dizzy. Hodes did not know them, but says the musicians who got press praise stopped playing with the traditional players.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: Well, I didn't know Charlie. And Dizzy came just after -- Dizzy and Charlie came in about 1947, and I didn't have anything to do with it then, didn't know them. But the other musicians that were getting plaudits, you didn't see them playing with us as much or anymore.

169.s: Old players didn't want to change, critics didn't understand.
169.ch: Bird's world, singers and the new music
169.q: : Oh yeah, they hated the newcomers. I don't know why. The old guys didn't want to learn nothing new. I guess that's basically what it really boils down to, is that they didn't want to change from their traditional things that they had been playing to play what the younger guys were playing. So I…

8.t: Basie, bebop, rock and another sit-in story
8.s: He did not like bebop or rock because it has no melody, and tells again of a union favor playing 'South Rampart Street Parade' with a rock band.
8.q: Well you see some of that music -- some of that music I didn't like at all, because I didn't know what they was playing --

428.t: Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker and the new sound
428.s: Dizzy sat in at the Black Cat, Hall knew Parker and Gillespie from Philadelphia and saw bebop as evolution.
428.q: I knew him in Philly. I knew him and I and 'Bama' [Carl WARWICK] Jimmy Hamilton knew Charlie in Philly, yeah, we came up, and --but, this was then a new sound and the guys were jamming at Minton's, but I was working in the studio then.

75.t: Bebop, Parker and Gillespie's audition for Kirby, the shuffle
75.s: He was never tuned to Bebop; Parker and Dizzy auditioned for Kirby, whose style was a shuffle; Louis Jordan the first Rock group.
75.q: I remember Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie auditioned for John Kirby's orchestra, but it wasn't their style. Kirby's was mostly a shuffle rhythm type of thing, while Charlie Parker and Dizzy were playing something else. Now, the shuffle is very important. It has a backbeat to it, it's a…

97.q: Bebop -- listen, real musicians didn't like any bebop. They didn't like bebop. They didn't like it, that's all there is to it. They didn't like it. And right now, it's so nice with the big bands coming back in again, because it was nothing but a gang of noise, repetition, repetition, repetition,…

86.t: Bebop-era changes: no left hand, no bass drum, experimental harmony
86.s: Edison describes how piano, drumming and harmony changed in the bop era and says he often could not understand the new records.
86.q: No. It was worse then than now. Now you wouldn't expect it but then you would expect it, you know. But you had the Bud Powells going then. You had the -- oh, let's see, who else was playing quite a bit around New York? Barry Harris, you had --

473.t: Dizzy shows him bebop harmonies; Cab bans it
473.s: After the firing Diz practised intensively and raved about Charlie Parker's chord substitutions; when both tried the ideas on "Some of These Days" Cab threatened to fire them, so Jones stuck to his commercial style, as he had a family.
473.q: Well, that's when he went into the woodshed. That's when he went in to practice, and he was already getting together with bebop.

98.t: Bebop was not danceable and singers took over
98.s: Saunders liked Parker and Gillespie but says bebop's tempos and runs could not be danced to, so the public drifted and recordings turned to singers fronting bands.
98.ch: Regal Theatre, bebop and the Woody Herman date
98.q: Well, the musician impression of it, I liked the music, and Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and all of these people who started in that era. But it wasn't danceable. This is why it didn't live. Outrageous tempos and the passages that they would play were -- a lot of execution and running and…

112.t: Indifference to bop; teaching Rae Harrison in his studio
112.s: He avoided bands after the Pleasure Beach affair, taught Rae Harrison in his studio and took her to Europe as manager and accompanist.
112.ch: New York choir and Rae Harrison
112.q: : I wasn't even interested in it. I'll tell you why, because as I told you, I didn't have any need to hear any band because I was through with black bands. You see, because the musicians after that Pleasure Beach Park episode, I
